gates.title: Per-image licensing, archive capture, and public availability

checks.claim: The image depicts genuine period Microsoft FreeCell, not the Vista+ remake or a clone.
checks.evidence: Read from the pixels at 1:1 and 4x. The title bar reads "FreeCell Game #14601" and the menu reads Game / Options / Help with "Cards Left: 52". The FreeCell king icon sits between the free cells and home cells. The chrome is Windows 3.x: a system-menu box, minimize/maximize arrows, no close button, and a dithered 16-colour title bar. Tut's Tomb, another Microsoft Entertainment Pack 2 game, is open behind FreeCell. Clones (GNOME, KDE, PySol, Marc L. Allen shareware) and the Windows 7-chrome capture were rejected; see provenance.json.

The pixels establish Windows 3.x-era Microsoft FreeCell. They cannot separate Windows 3.0 from 3.1, or the Entertainment Pack 2 binary from the Best of Entertainment Pack or Win32s builds. The Entertainment Pack 2 label is WinWorld's gallery caption, and the co-running Tut's Tomb supports it. Recorded as-is, not upgraded.
No capture date is published. The HTTP Last-Modified header reads 2015-10-02, which is a server file time. This is a later capture of period software (likely emulated), not a 1990s screenshot.

checks.claim: Original rights holder or creator recorded.
checks.evidence: Microsoft Corporation holds the software UI (FreeCell, Tut's Tomb, Windows 3.x). The screenshot capturer is not identified by WinWorld, and it is recorded as unknown rather than guessed.

The WinWorld gallery and detail pages carry no license. WinWorld's copyright page says copyright is retained by the original publisher even for abandoned software; its CC BY-SA 4.0 notice covers library descriptions only. Quoted exactly in rights.json.

checks.claim: The access method involved no account, payment, watermark removal or CAPTCHA.
checks.evidence: Anonymous public HTTPS GET, with response headers recorded. No watermark is present. No disk images or executables were downloaded or run at any point in the search.

checks.claim: The image is evidence of Visual Basic authorship or of VB shareware.
checks.evidence: FreeCell is a Microsoft product. It is period UI reference for what 1990s Windows card games looked like, and it is not evidence that any game was written in Visual Basic. Captions must not imply otherwise.

checks.claim: The asset may be used in the published video.
checks.evidence: Microsoft-copyrighted UI, unknown capturer, no license. Fair use is a legal-risk judgment. Handed off as review question XTRA-19-Q1.

gates.decision: Open. Unknown rights stay blocked per R14. No clearance recorded.

script_check.cue_text: Screenshots of 90s shareware card games — Solitaire, Hearts, FreeCell. Windows 3.1 and Windows 95 versions. The classic green felt background.

evidence: Microsoft KB Q106715 (Win32s 1.25a–1.30c, last reviewed 1998-05-21): "The installation guide for Win32s that is included in the Win32 SDK recommends running Freecell to verify that the installation was successful." Win32s is the 32-bit extension for Windows 3.1, so FreeCell shipped for Windows 3.1 systems with Win32s.

The WinWorld Entertainment Pack 2 product page says "Contains the games: Freecell, …" and "This version is for Windows 3.0 and later." Eli's Software Encyclopedia lists FreeCell on Entertainment Pack Volume 2, 1991, requiring Windows 3.1.

Internet Archive wep_best-of: the 1994 Best of Microsoft Entertainment Pack floppy, 'games for Windows 3.x', including FreeCell. Its screenshot-2 shows Free Cell in a German Windows 3.1 Program Manager.
The selected image itself shows FreeCell in Windows 3.x chrome.
checks.qualification: FreeCell was not part of Windows 3.1 itself. On Windows 3.x it was an add-on: Microsoft Entertainment Pack 2 (sold separately), the Best of Microsoft Entertainment Pack, and the Win32s test application. Keller's FAQ also says it was bundled with Windows for Workgroups; no Microsoft primary source for that was found. Microsoft first bundled FreeCell with Windows itself in Windows 95 (Keller FAQ; New York Times 2002 via the Wikipedia citation). No Microsoft primary file list for Windows 95 was located.

checks.evidence: 1991 per WinWorld and Eli's Software Encyclopedia; 1992 per Keller's FAQ ("first appeared in 1992 on Microsoft Entertainment Pack 2"). Neither is a Microsoft primary document. Do not put a year on screen without further evidence; "early 1990s" is supported by all three.

Microsoft FreeCell was commercial Microsoft software: sold on Entertainment Pack 2 and later bundled with Win32s and Windows 95. It was not shareware. (Jim Horne's earlier 1988 DOS FreeCell was shareware per Keller, but this is the Windows version.) The same holds for Microsoft Solitaire and Hearts. Line 593 of the narration correctly separates the bundled games from the shareware alternatives, so the visual cue's label contradicts the narration it sits beside.

script_check.result: Discrepancy in the visual-cue wording, not the narration. War/SCRIPT.md was not edited. Raised as review question XTRA-19-Q2 for the Writing Lead, with proposed wording in qa.md.
